slide.title: Four Questions Before Publishing
slide.body: A road with four signposts: Owner? · Licence? · Label? · True? It ends at a large 'Publish' button. Small tag: AI for Content Creators · Lesson 5.

scenes.voiceover: You made a campaign image with AI in two minutes. Before you publish it, can you answer four questions? Who owns it? Are you allowed to use it for business? Should you say it was made with AI? And is everything in the post true?

slide.title: Principles, not legal rules
slide.body: Large quote: "The law on AI and copyright is still developing, and it differs by country." Small note: High stakes? Ask your manager, client or a legal adviser.

scenes.voiceover: In the last lesson, we filtered our ideas down to a strong shortlist. Before we create anything, let's set some rules of the road. This lesson teaches principles and questions, not legal rules. The law on AI and copyright is still developing, and it is different from country to country. When the stakes are high, such as a large paid campaign, ask your manager, your client or a legal adviser.

slide.title: 1. Who owns it?
slide.body: Depends on where you are, and still changing · Add your own work: writing, editing, selecting, arranging · Using someone else's photo or text? You need the right to use it.

scenes.voiceover: The first question is, who owns it? The answer can depend on where you are, and it is still being decided in many places. A practical principle is this. The more of your own creative work you add, such as writing, editing, selecting and arranging, the stronger your position is likely to be. And if you upload someone else's photo or text, you need the right to use it.

slide.title: 2. Does the licence allow business use?
slide.body: Every tool has terms of use · Free and paid plans can differ · Read the current terms yourself · Record the date you checked

scenes.voiceover: The second question is, does the tool's licence allow commercial use? Every AI tool has terms of use. They say what you may do with the outputs, and they can differ between free and paid plans. Read the current terms yourself, and write down the date you checked, because terms change.

slide.title: 3. Should you label it?
slide.body: Check your platforms and your market. Example disclosure rule: "We label any image or video that is fully AI-generated and shows a realistic scene."

scenes.voiceover: The third question is, should you label it as made with AI? Check what your platforms and your market expect. Even where there is no rule, honesty protects trust. Many brands write a simple disclosure rule, for example: we label any image or video that is fully AI-generated and shows a realistic scene.

slide.title: 4. Is every claim checked?
slide.body: AI can invent: statistics · quotes · sources · product details → check each against a source you trust

scenes.voiceover: The fourth question is, is every fact and claim checked? AI can invent statistics, quotes, sources and product details. A false claim can mislead customers and damage their trust. So check every number, name, quote and claim against a source you trust.

scenes.on_screen_text: No imitation. No real people. No secrets.
scenes.voiceover: And some rules never change. Never imitate a named artist or an existing brand. Never use real people, logos or famous characters without permission. And never paste confidential or personal data into AI tools.

scenes.stock_query: car driving on open highway border
scenes.voiceover: Publishing is like driving across a border. The basic habits are the same everywhere, but the exact rules change by country and over time. A careful driver checks the local rules before each trip.
Let's follow Tomás. He runs marketing for a sample language school in Buenos Aires, Argentina. He plans to use a chat assistant, a design tool and a free image generator.

slide.title: Tomás's terms check
slide.body: Generic table, no real tool names: Tool type · Plan · Commercial use? · Conditions · Date checked. Row 3 (image generator, free plan) shows an amber 'Unclear: not for paid ads yet'.

scenes.voiceover: He reads the current terms of each tool, and for each one he notes the plan, whether commercial use is allowed, any conditions, and the date. For one image generator, he cannot find a clear answer about commercial use on the free plan. So he marks it unclear, and does not use it for paid ads until he confirms.

slide.title: The school's disclosure rule
slide.body: "Any realistic image or video that is fully generated by AI is labelled 'Created with AI'. Text drafted with AI and edited by our team does not need a label, unless a platform or local rule requires one." Footer: Review every 3 months.

scenes.voiceover: Then he writes the school's disclosure rule. Any realistic image or video that is fully generated by AI is labelled, created with AI. Text drafted with AI and edited by the team does not need a label, unless a platform or local rule asks for one. He will review the rule every three months.

slide.title: Check every claim
slide.body: Caption line struck through in red: "Students learn Spanish twice as fast with our method." Note: No evidence → removed.

scenes.voiceover: Finally, he checks a caption the AI wrote. It says students learn Spanish twice as fast with our method. The school has no evidence for this number. So he removes it.

A common mistake is to think, if the AI made it, it is free to use for anything. That is not safe. The opposite mistake is to avoid AI completely out of fear. The practical path is to check, record, add your own work, label where needed, and check every claim.

slide.title: Key takeaways
slide.body: 1. Four questions: owner, licence, label, true? 2. Answers differ and change: check current sources, record the date. 3. Disclosure rule + fact-checking = trust.

scenes.voiceover: Let's recap. First, before publishing, ask four questions: who owns it, does the licence allow commercial use, should it be labelled, and is every claim checked. Second, these answers differ by country and platform and change over time, so check current sources and record the date. Third, a written disclosure rule and a fact-checking habit protect your audience's trust.
